extracted.intended_audience: citizens, voters, and political actors debating slavery and popular sovereignty (mid-19th‑century U.S. political audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Rhetorical and evidentiary standards for arguing about slavery, Territorial governance, and the doctrine of popular sovereignty in mid‑19th century U.S. politics. Emphasizes historical accuracy, constitutional interpretation, logical consistency, and attention to practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical accuracy and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking the framers or the history of the country to support a political principle, present the whole controlling history (e.g., do not omit the Missouri Compromise or the Ordinance of '87).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes selective quotation and suppression of key events: "He selects parts of the history... and treats it as the whole, omitting... the Missouri Compromise" and the Ordinance of '87 which excluded slavery. Anti-pattern: relying on scattered quotations while suppressing the 'leading part and controlling feature' of history. Good practice: cite and account for major legislative acts and how founders actually acted, not only convenient fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat slavery as a durable, national question (not a trivial local matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not characterize slavery as a trivial, local, or purely economic question; treat it as a durable institution that can 'cannot be eradicated by the succeeding millions' and which has threatened the political existence of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts trivial local questions (who shall be governor, raising cattle) with the lasting consequences of planting slavery: "the durable, the important, and the mischievous one is, Shall this soil be planted with slavery?" Anti-pattern: likening slavery to garden pests or trivial property disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between Territories and States in constitutional and practical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments must account for legal and practical differences between Territories and States rather than treating them as 'exactly alike' in all respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question the claim that the Constitution applies to Territories 'precisely as it does to the States.' Examine why Territories are organized differently (e.g., lacking full representation, subject to congressional organization) and why that matters for questions like admitting slavery. Example issue: if Territories and States were identical, why not make Territories States at once?

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify when popular sovereignty applies (organization threshold and Congress's role)
rubrics_metrics.description: If asserting that 'the people' of a Territory decide slavery, specify when that popular sovereignty begins (Judge Douglas fix: 10,000–20,000 inhabitants) and who determines readiness (Douglas: Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out practical problems of the threshold (what about the nine thousand?) and the implication that Congress's control over organization can be used to delay or enable slavery. Good argument must address these mechanics and their political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose rhetorical substitutions and evasions (do not mask a term's meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of substituting neutral phrases (e.g., 'internal polity') for the specific institution at issue ('slavery') to evade controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker notes Douglas often uses 'internal polity' where 'slavery' would contradict his own history: such substitutions are deceptive. Guidance: use precise language and call out euphemisms that change the apparent stakes of an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consistency and honesty of position
rubrics_metrics.description: A defensible position must be internally consistent; avoid changing formulations to escape previously stated logical consequences (e.g., claiming both that Dred Scott affirms slave property and that Territories can exclude slavery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique highlights Douglas's shifting language on whether Territories can exclude slavery after Freeport. Anti-pattern: asserting incompatible claims or altering wording to avoid consequences rather than reconciling them through argument or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Supreme Court decisions by their explicit holdings and logical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on judicial decisions (e.g., Dred Scott), treat the decision's affirmations (such as the Constitution 'distinctly and expressly affirm[ing]' the right of slave property) and follow their logical implications (that such rights are embedded in the Constitution and limit Congressional or Territorial power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text summarizes Dred Scott: denying power to deprive property without due process and affirming slave property as constitutional. Good practice: accept and trace the decision's consequences (including that certain Territorial or state acts would be unconstitutional) rather than minimizing them as mere negatives or dicta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct from indirect legislative effects and assess constitutionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether 'unfriendly legislation' could lawfully exclude or destroy slave property, recognizing courts may strike down both direct and indirect attempts that amount to deprivation of property without due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker argues that while legislation framed to 'control as other property' might be sustained, direct or effectively indirect attempts to free or drive out slaves (taxing to death, declaring freedom) will be held unconstitutional by a court construing Dred Scott. Guidance: analyze both form and likely judicial response to proposed laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider practical political consequences of doctrines (who benefits / timing effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how a doctrine (e.g., popular sovereignty decided upon organization by Congress) would operate in practice and who would gain from delays or procedural controls (e.g., Southern interests using Congress to prevent Territories from acquiring popular sovereignty until admission as slave States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text points out that giving Congress the deciding power about when popular sovereignty attaches lets opponents stall until admission as a State, effectively nationalizing slavery. Good argument must trace such incentive structures and temporal tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base appeals to authority on what historical actors actually did, not on asserted sympathies
rubrics_metrics.description: When appealing to the framers or Revolutionary figures, show how they acted on the issue at hand rather than merely asserting they would have approved; use their concrete legislative choices as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker insists that if Judge Douglas claims the founders 'understood this question better,' he must show how they acted—e.g., their legislation excluding slavery—rather than merely citing their supposed abstract principles. Anti-pattern: invoking great names while ignoring their actual conduct.
